newsitem.title: USA: Rate worries depress stocks, bonds; dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Rate worries depress stocks, bonds; dollar falls.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks fell Monday as investors took profits after the market posted its biggest weekly gain ever last week and as bonds slid on fresh fears of higher interest rates.
The dollar dropped to a two-week low against the German mark as investors dumped most European currencies in favour of the relative safety of the German currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 43.34 points at 6,660.21, giving back some of the ground from last week's 312-point rally, which was the 30-stock index's largest weekly surge.

For the second time in as many weeks, the New York Stock Exchange handled its lowest trading volume of the year as only 393 million shares changed hands, barely beating the low of 407 million last Monday.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 1,649 to 905.

"The volume numbers tell you buyers have really backed away here," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It's not hard to figure out why. It's almost entirely a function of interest rates."
The 30-year Treasury bond was off 14/32, or $4.375 per $1,000 face value, raising its yield to 7.09 percent from Friday's close of 7.05 percent. The price and yield move in opposite directions.

Financial markets were again uneasy about another rise in interest rates after Federal Reserve Board Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin said the major threat to the economy at the moment was the possibility of over-heating.
"The major threat at the moment is not that the economy will run out of steam (but) that's always possible," Rivlin said in a speech to the Employment Policy Foundation.
"The thing that worries the Federal Reserve more is the possible overheating of the economy," she said.
The technology stocks were hammered again.

"The tech stocks participated in the rally last week for about 15 minutes," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "And this market is in a near-term downtrend regardless of last week's rally."
The dollar fell to 1.6965 German marks and 125.30 Japanese yen in late trading from 1.7118 marks and 125.89 yen late Friday.
Oil prices rose sharply as political turmoil threatened oil supplies in Nigeria and an Iraqi breach of a "no-fly" zone threatened that country's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for May delivery rose 47 cents a barrel to close at $20.38. May heating oil closed 0.80 cent a gallon higher at 55.48 cents, and May gasoline rose 1.31 cents to 62.80 cents.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices closed higher on worries about freeze damage to the winter wheat crop, flooding delays for spring wheat and persistent dryness in Europe that may shrink the crop there.
Wheat for delivery in May rose 2-1/2 cents a bushel to close at $4.39-1/2, its highest closing price since Aug. 13.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures set new life-of-contract highs across the board as optimism about future export demand to Asia following last month's halt of Taiwan's pork exports overcame a rise in reported supply.
Pork bellies for May delivery closed up 1.45 cents a pound at 91.40 cents.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index, which had risen 58.8 points the previous four sessions, ended 18.2 points higher at 4,328.7. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average finished 199.52 points or 1.09 percent higher at 18,551.66.
